first.why: Both pages describe the same Compound Polynomial multilevel growth-modeling method, combining within-year and between-year polynomial components to estimate seasonal student growth for school evaluation.

second.why: Both pages describe the same Compound Polynomial growth model developed by Thum and Hauser for jointly estimating within-year and between-year growth in a multilevel framework, serving the same purpose and practice.

first.why: Although both use value-added methods, A estimates school effects to identify effective schools for a principal-training award program, while B measures individual teachers’ contributions to student learning and access to effective teaching.
A concerns integrating additional data sources to address missing covariates, whereas B concerns exploring existing platform data to shape research questions, designs, and power calculations.
A focuses specifically on junction-tree estimation for multidimensional IRT growth models, whereas B presents the broader MML framework for multidimensional IRT models generally.
They are distinct collaborative-problem-solving frameworks with different component structures and emphases, even though both support analyzing or scaffolding collaborative problem solving.

Although both use Henmon’s P.E.-based normal-distribution scaling, one measures Latin sentence difficulty while the other assigns difficulty weights to individual vocabulary words, making them distinct methods.

Both describe Van der Vleuten’s utility framework as the same five-criterion method for appraising assessment instruments, despite applying it to different tool types and using slightly different criterion labels.

second.why: Both pages describe the same Van der Vleuten framework with identical criteria for evaluating assessment instruments, differing only in minor wording.
